q: Why do well-designed ML pipelines break the workflow into distinct, independently re-runnable stages, such as download, prepare, train and evaluate, tracked with recorded hashes of inputs and outputs, rather than one large monolithic script?
options: It lets the pipeline skip re-running stages whose inputs have not changed, and makes it possible to reproduce or debug any single stage without rerunning everything
It is required because monolithic single-file scripts cannot technically be written at all in the Python programming language used by most modern data science teams today
It automatically removes the need for a separate held-out test set anywhere in the overall pipeline design
It guarantees that every individual stage will produce exactly identical metrics no matter how many times it is rerun
explanation: Breaking the workflow into tracked, re-runnable stages allows unchanged stages to be skipped efficiently and makes it possible to isolate, reproduce and debug any single stage independently.

q: A credit-risk model needs a complete MLOps pipeline covering monitoring, retraining and validation. Which of the following pipeline designs best satisfies all three requirements together?
options: Continuously monitor live predictions and feature distributions for drift, automatically trigger retraining on fresh labelled data once drift and enough new data are present, and gate any retrained model behind a validation check before promotion
Monitor the model only once a year during a scheduled annual review, retraining it only if a team member happens to personally notice a problem with its live predictions sometime in between reviews

Retrain the model automatically every single day regardless of whether any meaningful drift has actually occurred, and promote every new version straight to production without ever running a validation check or comparing it against the prior deployed one
Validate the model thoroughly just once before its initial launch, and then skip any further monitoring, drift detection or retraining for the entire rest of its deployed production lifetime
explanation: Only the first option closes the loop across all three requirements: ongoing monitoring feeds a disciplined, data-driven retraining trigger, and every retrained candidate still passes a validation gate before replacing the production model.

q: A team deploys a recommendation model and considers the MLOps work finished once the API is live and serving predictions. What is missing from treating deployment as the final step?
options: Without ongoing monitoring and a feedback loop back into retraining, the team has no way to detect or respond to the model degrading as real-world conditions change
Nothing is actually missing here; deployment is always considered the final and complete step in any MLOps workflow
Deployment inherently includes fully automatic retraining built in, requiring no further monitoring, feedback loop or configuration from the team once the recommendation API has gone live
Monitoring after deployment is only ever necessary for models that specifically use deep learning architectures
explanation: Deployment is only one stage of the full loop; without monitoring and a path back into retraining, there is no way to notice or correct degradation once the model starts seeing real-world data.

q: Which of the following production scenarios best demonstrates a healthy, properly functioning end-to-end MLOps pipeline?
options: Monitoring detects rising drift, triggers a retraining job on new labelled data, the retrained model is validated against the current production model before being promoted, and a human reviews the change before it reaches all users
The model is never re-evaluated at all after its initial deployment, because the validation accuracy recorded at launch was already considered high enough to last indefinitely

A freshly retrained model is promoted directly to all production traffic immediately, without any comparison at all against the previous model's metrics, any validation gate, or any human review beforehand, regardless of how the retrained candidate actually performs
Monitoring alerts are generated correctly whenever drift occurs, but no defined process exists for anyone on the team to actually act on those alerts once they appear
explanation: A healthy pipeline closes the full loop: detection, retraining, validation against a quality bar, and human review before full promotion, which is exactly what the first scenario describes.
